en: The Śrī Viśvambharopaniṣad (The Upaniṣad of the Auspicious Sustainer of the Universe)

Then Śāṇḍilya asked Mahāśambhu: "Regarding that which has been described as 'from which words turn back, not having attained it along with the mind'—does that Brahman exist? Who is the sovereign Lord (Īśvara)? Who is beyond both the attributeless (nirguṇa) and the possessed-of-attributes (saguṇa)? Who is beyond both the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta)? And of what nature is the fashioner (Kartṛ)? Furthermore, by which mantras is the individual soul (jīva) immediately liberated from transmigratory existence? And who is entitled to the mastery of these mantras?"

Mahāśambhu said: "O Mahī, regarding that which you have asked—its name and form, its divine play, and its cit-filled abodes—which are indeed beyond the reach of mind and speech; by his own grace, these manifest themselves. Therefore, this self-ruling Rāghava is called 'Rūpanāman' (the one whose name is his form), for the eternal Brahman is the very light of his manifestation."

He who possesses attributes performs all the divine descents and pastimes; he himself, as Rāma in Ayodhyā, performs the *rāsa* dance. Of that Supreme Person, who is beyond both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*), the sounds of the mantra and its *nāda* and *bindu* are beyond the reach of speech and mind. His mantras are infinite, among which six hundred are most excellent, and among those, three mantras are preeminent.

The six-syllabled mantra known as the "Pair" (*dvayākhya*) consists of the jewel-mantra preceded by the *bindu* (the syllable *oṃ*), followed by the long *agni* (the syllable *ra*), then the long *agni* alone, then *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), then *atha-prathana-mai* (the syllable *thaiṃ*), then first *śrīmad*, then *rāmacandra-caraṇau*, then one should say the word *śaraṇam*, after which one should say *prapadye*, and again *śrīmate*. Then *rāmacandrāya*, and before that [word], *namaḥ*. This is the most excellent of all mantras, the mantra known as the "Pair" belonging to the son of Daśaratha.

"One who studies this jewel attains all desires and rejoices together with it. Now, following the *praṇava*, there is no second syllable; *sa* is the third syllable, *cī* is the fourth syllable, *tā* is the fifth syllable, *ra* is the sixth syllable, *ma* is the seventh syllable, and *bhyāma* is the eighth syllable. One who knows this eight-syllabled [mantra] becomes liberated. Having recited these three mantras—the best of all mantras—one is immediately released from the bondage of karma. He who possesses supreme devotion to Śrī Rāma alone is qualified for this mantra.

Śrī Rāma alone is the cause of all; his form is twofold: limited and unlimited. Abiding in the Forest of Delight (Pramoda-vana) at Sāketa in his limited form, he performs the *rāsa* dance itself. His second form is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. From his right side emerged the one who reclines upon the salt ocean; from his left side emerged Ramā, the resident of Vaikuṇṭha. From his heart arose Para-Nārāyaṇa, and from his two feet came the one who dwells in the Badarikā forest. From his aesthetic grace (*śṛṅgāra*) came Nanda-nandana.

In this way, all incarnations emerge from the footprints of Śrī Rāmacandra; likewise, infinite crores of Viṣṇus and the Caturvyūha emerge. Similarly, Aparājiteśvara and immeasurable Paranārāyaṇas and others, as well as infinite crores of eight-armed Nārāyaṇas, always worship him with palms joined in reverence. Whenever he commands Viṣṇu and the others, they perform all the tasks within that universe. All of them [do so].

O Śrī Raghuvara, the gods are of two kinds—those who are distinct portions and those who are non-distinct portions—and both serve you; the distinct portions are Brahmā and others, while the non-distinct portions are Nara and others.

For a thousand years they perform the five-limbed worship (*pañcāṅgopāsanā*) of the individual soul (*jīvātman*), and thereby they become of the nature of bliss. Then, [the scripture says]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. First, those who practice the five-limbed worship, having performed the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa at the time of creation, attain Goloka. There, some remain in that very place, while others become qualified for the worship of Rāma. Having entered into superior bodies such as those of Viṣṇu, he becomes a deity; yet, remaining within inferior mortal bodies, he worships the deities.

Of Him who is higher than the highest, named Śrī Rāma, all names such as Nārāyaṇa and others are derived; from His abode their abodes arise, from His pastimes all pastimes manifest, and from His essential nature all forms appear. He alone is the Lord of lords, the primordial cause of all causes; there is no reality whatsoever higher than Him.

Now the Yantra is described in detail: O Rāma, for those seekers of liberation who have attained [this path], there is no perfection of the mantras dedicated to the divine Self without the Yantra. Because it restrains (yantraṇā) defects such as desire, anger, and the like, it is called a "Yantra"; and because it effects restraint (yamanāt), it is also called a "Yantra. First, a hexagon should be drawn; then one should draw a circle. Eight petals should be drawn, and after that, a square.

One should surround this yantra of mine—which is endowed with all auspicious marks, divine, and the bestower of all happiness—with the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of all the incarnations (*avatāra*). Then, one should always perform the worship of this yantra. In its center, one should clearly draw the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) according to the prescribed ritual, and then one should write the seed-syllable, having first enclosed it within that [object].

Then, the wise one should perform the repetition of those five seed-syllables; furthermore, he should cause them to be worshipped with the ten-syllable mantra. He should write the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in order within the corners starting from the southeast. Again, the intelligent one should write *hīṃ* and *śrīṃ* on the cheeks of the corners. At the tip of each corner, the seed-syllable *huṃ* is to be written, and in the filaments (*keśara*), the garland of letters known as the "mind" (*manonmanī*) is prescribed. There are forty-seven letters: seven letters thus [placed] on the petals, six on each of the first five petals, and eight on the eighth petal.

In the eastern half, the knower of all principles should worship with the letters beginning with *ka* and so forth; he should correctly inscribe the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Narasiṃha and Vārāha. In the four directions and intermediate points, starting from the east, one should draw a square earth-pavilion (*bhūgṛha*). By worshipping this yantra, a person shall obtain both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

Alternatively, one should write the seed-syllable *TĀR* (Om) in the center, and likewise the letters of the Śrī Rāma mantra in sequence within the six corners. One should place the *Aṅga-mantra* at the joints (*sandhi*) and the *Mānmatha* (Klīm) at the lobes (*gaṇḍa*). Similarly, one should inscribe the *Māyā* (Hrīm) on the filaments (*kiñjalka*). As before, one should write the *Mālā-mantra* in sequence upon the petals. Then, having encircled it with the ten-syllabled mantra, one should write the consonants beginning with *Ka*. Likewise, one should place the seed-syllables of Narasiṃha and Vārāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions. This other Yantra, complete with its limbs and coverings, should be worshipped according to the prescribed ritual. Having drawn it either on silver, gold, or birch bark, one should worship it.

*Huṃ jānakīvallabhāya svāhā kṣauṃ*. One should recite this again. The ten-syllable mantra of Vārāha and Narasiṃha is recorded as follows: one should first say *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*, and immediately thereafter say the word *namaḥ*. Then one should utter the word *bhagavate*, followed by the word *raghunandanāya*. After that, [one says] *rakṣoghnaviśadāya*, then the word *madhureṇa*, and subsequently one should say *prasanna*. Then one should utter the word *vadanāya*, followed by *amitatejase*. After that, one should recite *balāya rāmāya viṣṇave*.

*Namaḥ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīñcoṃ namo bhagavate raghunandanāya rakṣoghna viśadāya madhura prasanna vadanāya amita tejase balāya rāmāya viṣṇave namaḥ.* This is declared to be the *mālā-mantra*, which bestows the desired objects upon those who contemplate it.

"Oṃ sīṃ, [salutation] to Sītā"—this is declared to be the mantra of Sītā. Having propitiated Rāma along with his limbs (aṅgas) and his retinues (āvaraṇas) through this mantra, and having likewise propitiated [the deity], one should fashion a pill and wear the yantra daily. It pacifies all miseries for men and bestows sons and grandsons; it eternally grants all branches of knowledge and always produces every happiness. Indeed, in matters of warding off others' spells and incantations, it is like an adamantine cage (vajrapañjara).

What need is there for much speaking? [This] bestows all perfections upon men and destroys their grief. The supreme practitioner, having properly installed the Yantra according to the prescribed rite, should worship Gaṇeśa and the other deities, as well as all the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), who stand before the pedestal of the doorway of Śrī Rāma in the form of his retinue. Having first purified his own body, he should thereafter perform the worship. The wise man should sacrifice to the deities with sixteen, eleven, or five offerings, according to his own capacity.

One should recite the mantra of Rāma, who is endowed with all powers, along with His limbs (Aṅgas) and enclosures (Āvaraṇas). Out of devotion, one should praise all the attendants for the sake of pleasing Rāma. The person who performs the worship of the King of Yantras in this manner attains desired happiness in this world and, after death, reaches Sāketa.

Of this mantra for taking refuge in Śrī Rāma: Śrī Rāmacandra is the Seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the metre (chandaḥ), the Supreme Soul Śrī Rāmacandra is the deity (devatā), *rāṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), and *namaḥ* is the power (śakti). Its application (viniyoga) is in recitation (*japa*) for the attainment of all desired aims. Having performed the purification of the hands with the root-mantra, one should first place the seed-syllable upon the palms of both hands; the remaining syllables should be placed upon the joints of the fingers.

To the two big toes of the glorious Rāmacandra, *namaḥ*; to the two index fingers, refuge, *namaḥ*; I take refuge in the two middle fingers, *namaḥ*; to the glorious one, to the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*; to Rāmacandra, to the two little fingers, *namaḥ*; to the palms and backs of the hands, *namaḥ*. To the two feet of Śrīrāmacandra, for knowledge, *namaḥ* to the heart; refuge, for sovereignty, *svāhā* to the head; I take refuge, for power, *vaṣaṭ* to the tuft of hair; to the glorious one, for strength, *huṃ* to the armor; to Rāmacandra.

To the splendor of the two eyes, *bauṣaṭ*; obeisance to the seed-syllable, *phaṭ*. To the feet of Śrī Rāmacandra for knowledge, obeisance to the belly; for refuge to sovereignty, obeisance to the back; I take refuge in power, obeisance to the two arms; to the illustrious one for strength, obeisance to the two thighs; to Rāmacandra for splendor, obeisance to the two knees; obeisance to valor, obeisance to the two feet. Now, the placement upon the body (*dehanyāsa*): *śrīṃ* obeisance, *ma* obeisance, *rāṃ* obeisance, *na* obeisance, *ma* obeisance, *ca* obeisance, *dra* obeisance, *caṃ* obeisance, *raṃ* obeisance, *ṇauṃ* obeisance.

*Śaṃ namaḥ, raṃ namaḥ, ṇaṃ namaḥ, praṃ namaḥ, paṃ namaḥ, dyaṃ namaḥ, śrīṃ namaḥ, maṃ namaḥ, namaḥ, rāṃ namaḥ, maṃ namaḥ, caṃ namaḥ, drāṃ namaḥ, yaṃ namaḥ, naṃ namaḥ, moṃ namaḥ.* One should thus perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) above [the head]. *Śrīṃ* on the head; *mū* on the forehead; *ma* on the eyes; *te* on the ears; *bha* on the nose; *lā* on the mouth; *ra* on the two arms; *ṇa* on the heart; *pra* on the two breasts; *pa* on the navel; *dya* on the back; *śrī* on the two shanks; *ma* on the two calves; *te* on the hips; *jā* on the two thighs; *ca* on the knees; *ndrā* on the feet; *ya* on the feet; *na* on the feet; *maḥ* on the feet.

Now, the meditation: For the attainment of all desired goals, one should meditate upon Rāma together with Jānakī; he has the luster of an indranīla gem, holds the *jñānamudrā*, is adorned with all ornaments, has his bow and arrows resting at his side, possesses every beautiful limb, and has lotus-like eyes.

Oṃ, salutations to the two thumbs; salutations to the two index fingers; salutations to Sītā and Rāma with the two middle fingers; Oṃ, salutations to the two ring fingers; salutations to the two little fingers; salutations to Sītā and Rāma with the palms and backs of the hands. Oṃ, salutations to Jñāna (Knowledge) for the heart; salutations to Aiśvarya (Sovereignty) for the head, Svāhā; salutations to Sītā and Rāma for Śakti (Power) for the tuft of hair, Vaṣaṭ; Oṃ, salutations to Bala (Strength) for the armor; salutations to Tejas (Splendor) for the eyes; salutations to Sītā and Rāma for Vīrya (Vigor) for the weapon, Phaṭ. The meditation is as before.

Of this six-syllabled king of mantras of Śrī Rāma, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī Rāma is the deity (devatā), *rāṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *namaḥ* is the power (śakti), and *rāmāya* is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in recitation for the sake of pleasing Śrī Rāma.

Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi); [place] on the head. Oṃ, salutation to the Gāyatrī meter (chandas); [place] on the mouth. Oṃ, salutation to the deity Rāṃ; [place] on the heart. Oṃ, salutation to the seed-syllable (bīja) Rāṃ; [place] on the private parts. Oṃ, salutation to the power (śakti); [place] on the feet. Oṃ, salutation to the pin (kīlaka) Rāmāya; [place] on all limbs. Oṃ Rāṃ, salutation to the two thumbs. Oṃ Rīṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers. Oṃ Rūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers. Oṃ Raiṃ, huṃ to the two ring fingers. Oṃ Rauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers. Oṃ Ra; [conclude].

*Phaṭ* with both palms and the backs of the hands. *Oṃ rāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ rīṃ śirase svāhā*, *oṃ rūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ raiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *oṃ rauṃ netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ raḥ astrāya phaṭ*. *Rāṃ namaḥ* at the *brahmarandhra*; *rāṃ namaḥ* between the eyebrows; *māṃ namaḥ* in the heart; *yaṃ namaḥ* at the navel; *naṃ namaḥ* at the *liṅga*; *man namaḥ* at the feet; *rāṃ namaḥ* on the head; *rāṃ namaḥ* on the face; *māṃ namaḥ* in the heart; *yaṃ namaḥ* at the navel; *naṃ namaḥ*.

*Guhye maṃ namaḥ*, *pādayoḥ rāṃ namaḥ*, *nābhau se namaḥ*, *guhye māṃ namaḥ*, *pādayoḥ rāṃ namaḥ*, *śirasi naṃ namaḥ*, *mukhe maṃ namaḥ*, *hṛdaye rāṃ namaḥ*, *pādayoḥ rāṃ namaḥ*, *guhye māṃ namaḥ*. (With the commentary in the vernacular.)

*Namaḥ* at the navel; *na-namaḥ* at the heart; *man-namaḥ* at the mouth; *rāṃ namaḥ* at the head; *rāṃ namaḥ* at the head; *māṃ namaḥ* at the mouth; *yaṃ namaḥ* at the heart; *yaṃ namaḥ* at the navel; *naṃ namaḥ* at the private parts; *maṃ namaḥ* at the feet; *saṃ namaḥ* at the navel; *rāṃ namaḥ* at the private parts; *māṃ namaḥ* at the feet; *yaṃ namaḥ* at the head; *naṃ namaḥ* at the mouth; *maṃ namaḥ* at the heart; *rāṃ namaḥ* at the head; *rāmāya namaḥ* at the navel; *namo namaḥ* at the feet.

Having first performed the purification of the body, one should worship the Joy of the Raghus. Having purified the articles of worship, one should cleanse the vessels for worship. With well-sprinkled materials, one should properly worship Puruṣottama. When Rāma is propitiated according to the prescribed rite, he becomes truly worshipped. Then, having swept the temple, one should invoke the omnipresent Lord. Having invoked the Lord of Gods, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) in the center; then one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and thereafter bathe the Lord with the waters of the Sarayū and other rivers during the festival of Sītā.

One should properly offer garments and likewise offer the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*). Then, having offered body-unguents (*aṅgarāga*), one should offer a garland of *tulasī* flowers. Thereafter, one should adorn the two-armed Lord with all ornaments. One should worship His limbs properly; then Rāma becomes pleased. One should offer incense, a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), and a waving of lights (*ārārtika*). Then one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and perform circumambulation. One should prostrate according to the scriptural injunctions and praise the Supreme beyond the supreme with hymns of praise.

Whoever worships in this manner attains immortality. This, however, is the supreme secret, a mystery difficult for all to obtain; it should be given to a devotee of Rāma, but must not be given to an ordinary person.
Thus ends the Viśvambharopaniṣad in the Atharvaveda.
